meta.title: Who really said "Far better it is to dare mighty things, to win glorious triumphs, even though checkered by failure, than to rank with those poor spirits who neither enjoy much nor suffer much, because they live in the gray twilight that knows neither victory nor defeat"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Yes — Theodore Roosevelt, at Chicago’s Hamilton Club on 10 April 1899. But he said “take rank with” and “knows not victory nor defeat.”

answer.sourceLine: Roosevelt said it in “The Strenuous Life,” his address to the Hamilton Club of Chicago on 10 April 1899, collected in The Strenuous Life: Essays and Addresses (The Century Co., 1900). The printed speech reads “than to take rank with those poor spirits” and “the gray twilight that knows not victory nor defeat” — the circulating version drops a word and smooths the ending.

source.excerpt: As it is with the individual, so it is with the nation. It is a base untruth to say that happy is the nation that has no history. Thrice happy is the nation that has a glorious history. Far better it is to dare mighty things, to win glorious triumphs, even though checkered by failure, than to take rank with those poor spirits who neither enjoy much nor suffer much, because they live in the gray twilight that knows not victory nor defeat.
trail: The line sits in the fourth paragraph of the address printed under the heading “SPEECH BEFORE THE HAMILTON CLUB, CHICAGO, APRIL 10, 1899” in Project Gutenberg’s text of The Strenuous Life ↗, volume 12 of The Works of Theodore Roosevelt.
The Theodore Roosevelt Center ↗ gives the same wording — “take rank,” “knows not victory nor defeat” — and sources it to The Strenuous Life, Hamilton Club, 1899.

The University of Maryland’s Voices of Democracy transcription of the speech ↗ independently carries “Far better it is to dare mighty things, to win glorious triumphs, even though checkered by failure” and dates the address 10 April 1899.
Wikipedia’s article on the speech ↗ confirms Roosevelt delivered it in Chicago on 10 April 1899 as Governor of New York, and that it was published in 1900 in a collection of the same name.

author.bio: Theodore Roosevelt was a historian, naturalist, Rough Rider colonel and relentless author as well as a politician. He delivered “The Strenuous Life” as Governor of New York, an office he held from 1899 to 1900; he became the 26th U.S. President on 14 September 1901 and served until 1909. His speeches were collected and reprinted constantly in his own lifetime, which is one reason his name still attracts so many quotations — genuine and otherwise.

misattribution.heading: The attribution is right. The wording is not.
misattribution.intro: Nobody else is seriously credited with this sentence — Roosevelt really did say it, and the source is a documented speech. The trouble is that the version everyone repeats has been quietly edited in transit, and the edits have spread into reference works that ought to know better.

items.who: “than to rank with those poor spirits”
items.why: Roosevelt said “than to take rank with those poor spirits.” The verb survives intact in the Project Gutenberg text of The Strenuous Life ↗ and in the Theodore Roosevelt Center’s record ↗.

The printed speech ends “because they live in the gray twilight that knows not victory nor defeat.” The tidier “knows neither… nor” construction is a later improvement on Roosevelt, not his phrasing — compare the full text of the address ↗.

Wikiquote lists the line under its sourced section for The Strenuous Life: Essays and Addresses ↗, but prints “than to rank with … because they live in that grey twilight that knows neither victory nor defeat” — three departures at once from the printed speech: the missing “take,” “that grey” for “the gray,” and the reworked ending.

BrainyQuote’s page ↗ inverts the opening to “Far better is it,” cuts the middle with an ellipsis, drops a “much” from “neither enjoy much nor suffer much,” reads “a gray twilight,” and names no speech, book, or date at all.

misattribution.truthLine: Roosevelt said it — on 10 April 1899, to the Hamilton Club of Chicago. What he actually said was: “Far better it is to dare mighty things, to win glorious triumphs, even though checkered by failure, than to take rank with those poor spirits who neither enjoy much nor suffer much, because they live in the gray twilight that knows not victory nor defeat,” as printed in The Strenuous Life ↗.

context.heading: Written about nations, borrowed by individuals
lead: Roosevelt was still Governor of New York, two offices short of the presidency, when he stood before Chicago’s Hamilton Club on 10 April 1899 and announced that he wished to preach “not the doctrine of ignoble ease, but the doctrine of the strenuous life.” The famous sentence is not the personal-ambition slogan it has become. It arrives in a passage about nations — immediately after “It is a base untruth to say that happy is the nation that has no history” — and runs straight on into a defence of the Union’s decision to fight in 1861.

That framing is almost always stripped off in circulation. The speech was an expansionist argument by a recent Rough Rider urging an America fresh from war with Spain to accept the costs of empire rather than shrink from them; the line about the gray twilight was his rebuke to a country he thought tempted by comfort, not advice to an individual weighing a career move.
context.detailsSummary: Where you have probably met the phrase lately
detailsBody: “Dare mighty things” is the unofficial motto of NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory, and JPL engineers encoded the phrase in binary into the orange-and-white pattern of the Perseverance Mars rover’s parachute, alongside the GPS coordinates of JPL’s headquarters in Pasadena. Wikipedia’s account of the rover ↗ records both the coded phrase and the motto, and notes the phrase is attributed to Roosevelt.
